title: Discernment is the way (2.26–2.28)
hook: the cure is to tell the seer from the seen, not once in a flash but steadily, and the limbs of yoga make the light grow

segments.voice: Yesterday: apavarga, and your line, for the seer. Experience and liberation, both. Did one ordinary thing get fully tasted, then let go? Day four hundred fifty-six.

Identical twins walk into a room. Strangers mix them up all evening. Their teacher gets it right most days. Their mother never gets it wrong, not even from behind, not even half asleep. She didn't learn that in one moment of insight. She learned it over years of ordinary mornings, until telling them apart stopped being an effort and became the way she sees. Patanjali has named the disease and its cause. Today he names the cure and the remedy, and the remedy works a lot like that mother's eyes.
screen: `IDENTICAL TWINS.` → `STRANGERS MIX THEM UP.` → `THEIR MOTHER NEVER DOES.`

segments.voice: First the cure. Sutras 2.23 to 2.25 trace the knot: the seer and the seen are joined because of avidya, not seeing clearly. Take away the not-seeing, and the joining falls apart. Patanjali calls that removal the seer's aloneness. Freedom. Then sutra 2.26 gives the remedy. Viveka-khyati, aviplava. Viveka means discernment, telling one thing from another, the way a jeweler tells gold from brass. Khyati is the clear seeing of it. And aviplava is the word to circle: unwavering. Not a flash on a mountaintop that's gone by Monday. Steady. The mother's eyes, not the stranger's lucky guess. Sutra 2.27 says that for the one with this steady discernment, wisdom arrives in seven stages, all the way to the end. The sutra doesn't list them. The classical commentary does. Then 2.28 sets up the rest of the book. By practicing the limbs of yoga, impurity dwindles, and the light of knowledge shines brighter, all the way to discernment. A lamp with a sooty glass doesn't need more flame. It needs the glass wiped, again and again. So the long list that starts tomorrow, the eight limbs, isn't a set of rules for their own sake. It's how the glass gets wiped. In daily life, viveka is tiny and practical: this is a thought, not a fact. This is my mood, not who I am. Said once, it's a flash. Said every day, it becomes how you see.
screen: `THE CURE: NO MORE NOT-SEEING.` · `VIVEKA — TELLING APART.` · `AVIPLAVA — UNWAVERING.` · `THE LIMBS WIPE THE SOOTY GLASS.` · then, large: `VIVEKA.`

segments.voice: Today's practice trains the unwavering part, aviplava. Sit and let the breath settle. Count the out-breaths, one to ten, then start again. When a thought pulls you off count, notice it plainly: a thought, not a fact. Then go back to one. Losing count isn't failure. Noticing that you lost it is the discernment, and coming back, again and again, is the steadiness. The bell holds the time.
Aviplava. Unwavering discernment between seer and seen, held so steady it stops wavering.
Your line: viveka. Today, when a hard thought shows up, try one quiet sentence: this is a thought, not a fact. Say it again the next time too. Day four hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: In the Yoga tradition, discernment between awareness and what it is aware of is the central means of liberation, cultivated over years through study, the ethical disciplines and meditation, usually under a teacher's guidance.

match.prompt: the cure and the remedy — tap the pairs.

myth: for Patanjali, one flash of insight is enough
2.26 asks for discernment that is unwavering, aviplava.
the sutra on seven stages of wisdom doesn't list them
2.27 names seven stages; the classical commentary spells them out.
the limbs of yoga make the light of knowledge shine brighter
2.28: as impurity dwindles, the light shines all the way to discernment.

fork.setup: you've had a moment of seeing clearly: you are not your passing moods. by Monday it's faded. what does Patanjali point you to?
options: decide the first one was fake.
practice the limbs until the seeing stops wavering.
fork.reveal: 2.26 asks for unwavering discernment, and 2.28 says it grows by practicing the limbs of yoga as impurity dwindles.

original.note: Sanskrit viveka: discernment, discrimination, telling one thing from another; in 2.26, viveka-khyāti.

trapdoor: what you thought: discernment means good taste or careful judgment.
what it means: telling the seer from the seen, held so steadily it never wavers, is the remedy for suffering.
what a scholar hears: viveka-khyatir aviplava hanopayah (2.26), the remedy that completes the medical fourfold; 2.28 makes the eight limbs the means of that discernment.

sources.ref: Yoga Sutra 2.23–2.25 (avidya causes the conjunction; its removal is the seer's aloneness)
Yoga Sutra 2.26 (unwavering discriminative discernment is the means of removal)
Yoga Sutra 2.27–2.28 (sevenfold wisdom; the limbs of yoga and the light of knowledge)

notes: Sanskrit of 2.26 given as viveka-khyatir aviplava hanopayah; confirm.
The sooty lamp-glass image is the script's illustration, not a quotation from the commentary.
The seven stages of 2.27 are listed in the Yoga Bhashya; not named in the script to keep one idea.

Editor review (2026-10-01): replaced the counted 'ten thousand mornings', a husk image that repeated day 453, a 'think of' cue and the stock 'ordinary Tuesday'; the practice no longer repeats the seen/seer noting of days 454-455 and now trains steadiness (aviplava) by counting breaths.
